rows.Title: PIR – Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise – Increased request latency and command timeouts
rows.What happened: Between 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 and 23:50 UTC on 08 September 2026, a platform issue impacted Azure Managed Redis and Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise. Affected customers may have experienced periodic increases in request latency and command timeouts during recurring infrastructure activities, with the impact more pronounced for workloads hosted on smaller virtual machines.
rows.What went wrong and why: 23:36 UTC on 27 July 2026 – Customer impact began following deployment of the updated security-related component.
rows.How did we respond: We are enhancing monitoring capabilities to enable faster detection of significant increases in infrastructure CPU utilization that may affect latency and command processing. (Estimated completion: November 2026)
rows.How are we making incidents like this le: There was nothing that customers could have done to avoid or minimize impact from this specific service incident.
rows.How can customers make incidents like th: You can rate this PIR and provide any feedback using our quick 3-question survey: Customer feedback survey (8Q1S-GLG)

rows.Title: PIR – Azure Managed Redis – Intermittent Server Load Metric Spikes and Increased Latency on Affected Cache Instances
rows.What happened: Between 14:00 UTC on 15 May 2026 and 22:43 UTC on 20 July 2026, a platform issue affected customers using Azure Managed Redis in multiple regions. Following a scheduled maintenance update, a subset of Azure Managed Redis caches experienced periodic spikes in Server Load and CPU utilization to approximately 100% at 10-minute intervals. Customers using smaller cache SKUs (B0, B1, B2, B3, B5, M10, X3, and X5, which use 2-vCPU nodes) may have also experienced brief latency increases lasting approximately 12–15 seconds during these periodic events. In some cases, internal management operations on affected caches were temporarily delayed or blocked; however, data-plane operations, including client connections and read/write requests, continued to function normally.
rows.What went wrong and why: A scheduled maintenance update introduced a change to the way internal diagnostic log collection operated within the Redis engine. Under specific conditions, multiple diagnostic collection processes executed simultaneously at regular 10-minute intervals. On smaller cache SKUs using 2-vCPU nodes, the additional processing briefly consumed available CPU resources for approximately 12–15 seconds, resulting in periodic spikes in Server Load and CPU utilization. Because the Server Load metric reports the highest CPU utilization observed during each measurement interval, these brief periods of elevated utilization appeared as recurring spikes to approximately 100%. Larger cache SKUs, which have additional CPU resources available, experienced the same diagnostic activity but were able to absorb the additional processing without observable customer impact.
rows.How did we respond: 14:00 UTC on 15 May 2026 – Customer impact began as the scheduled maintenance update started rolling out across regions.
rows.How are we making incidents like this le: We have implemented a fleet-wide mitigation that staggers the execution of internal diagnostic processes on affected Azure Managed Redis caches, preventing the simultaneous activity that caused the periodic resource utilization spikes. Newly created caches are provisioned with the corrected service version. (Completed)
rows.How can customers make incidents like th: Consider using the CPU metric (percentProcessorTime) instead of Server Load when monitoring Azure Managed Redis cache health and configuring alerts. The CPU metric provides a more representative view of sustained resource utilization, while the Server Load metric can reflect short-duration transient spikes. When viewing Server Load in the Azure portal, consider using the Average aggregation rather than Maximum (Max) for a more representative view of resource utilization. For additional guidance, see Azure Managed Redis Server Load best practices: https://aka.ms/amr/serverload-best-practices

rows.Title: PIR – Azure Monitor Action Groups – Email Action Notification Failures
rows.What happened: Between 17:21 UTC and 21:17 UTC on 22 July 2026, a platform issue affected the Action Groups email notifications within Azure Monitor in multiple regions. Impacted customers may have experienced degraded service performance, including failures delivering email notifications when email actions were invoked.
rows.What went wrong and why: The issue was caused by reliability problems affecting a downstream email delivery service called MEO (Microsoft Email Orchestrator) used by the Azure Notification Service to process Action Groups email notifications. During the incident, the downstream service experienced unhealthy service instances, resulting in increased request timeouts when processing email notification requests. As a result, some Action Groups email notifications could not be processed successfully, leading to notification delivery failures for impacted customers.
rows.How did we respond: 17:21 UTC on 22 July 2026 – Customer impact began.
rows.How are we making incidents like this le: We are improving the service to be more resilient to temporary timeout conditions, helping ensure email notifications continue to be delivered successfully even when dependent services experience transient delays. (Estimated completion: August 2026)
rows.How can customers make incidents like th: Consider setting up multiple types of mechanisms to get notifications - app push, phone call, SMS, webhook and more. Create and manage action groups in Azure Monitor - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn
